newsitem.title: USA: Clinton praises Republican flexibility on taxes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton praises Republican flexibility on taxes.

text.p: Republican leaders papered over differences within their ranks Tuesday as President Clinton welcomed signs of flexibility on tax cuts which he said would make it easier to attain a balanced budget.

The president welcomed flexibility shown by House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who stirred the budget debate Monday with suggestions that one of his party's most prized goals, a major tax cut, could be held off until the budget is balanced.
He invited House and Senate budget leaders of both parties to the White House Wednesday to discuss where to go next on reaching a five-year deal to balance the budget.

"We have to seize this opportunity to pass a bipartisan agreement to balance the budget," Clinton told reporters at the White House. "There are now some new and hopeful signs that we are in a position to do that."

Clinton said he was taking three steps to move the budget process forward -- inviting the budget committee leaders to meet him Wednesday, asking his budget team to hold talks with congressional budget leaders during the congressional recess and asking them to report back afterward at the White House.

Faced with internal dissent over Gingrich's comments, House and Senate Republican leaders held a joint news conference in which they affirmed support for tax cuts and said the dispute was only procedural.

Gingrich's views on taxes differed sharply from other Republicans, including a group of 28 conservative Republicans who warned in a letter to House Republican leaders that a postponement could doom chances for winning the tax cuts.

"Rather than folding, some members ought to exercise leadership, drive a message and fight for a principle. Otherwise what's the point of being in the majority?" the group's leader, Representative David McIntosh of Indiana said.

The chief Senate tax writer, Finance Chairman William Roth, also sought to quickly head off the talk of no tax cut. The Delaware Republican unveiled a plan to balance the budget in five years with a $178 billion tax cut. It would be mainly paid for by reining in the cost of living increases paid to retirees, extensions of current taxes and other small tax hikes.

Republicans have recommended nearly $200 billion in tax cuts over five years -- about twice the amount requested by Clinton, who also insists that they be targeted to things he wants to promote such as higher education. The Republican plan includes a costly reduction in the capital gains tax.
The disarray among Republicans delighted Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle. "There seems to be an internal civil war going on," the South Dakota Democrat said.

Gingrich's shift on taxes dovetailed easily with that of an influential group of House Democrats who hold that no tax cut should take place until the budget is balanced. Representative John Spratt, the ranking Democrat on the House Budget Committee, will continue his warning against using a lower consumer price index to finance the tax cuts, an aide said.

Senate Budget Comittee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, Wednesday will open formal discussions of the fiscal 1998 budget with a discussion of what programmes are in the budget. He threatened to bring up his own plan with steep spending cuts and no tax cut unless negotiations start soon. A tax cut could be voted on separately from the spending cut portion of the budget, but under the same procedures which would prevent it being blocked on the Senate floor, he said.

Republicans say Clinton's budget proposal would result in a $69 billion deficit in 2002, the year the president said it would balance. They have also protested over Clinton's "unwillingness" to address the consumer price index issue as an obstacle to serious budget negotiations.
